entry.evidence: We revisit the question of MICI in the AIS using a more complex parameterization of cliff calving

steps.action: Names the collapse and calving of exposed ice cliffs after ice-shelf loss as a major uncertainty in Antarctic sea-level projections.
steps.quote: One such uncertainty is the potential collapse and the calving of large ice cliffs

steps.action: Takes the MICI concept from published stress analyses of ice-cliff stability (self-reinforcing cliff failure as the grounding line retreats).
steps.quote: This is referred to as Marine Ice Cliff Instability (MICI)

steps.action: Cites the DeConto and Pollard (2016) projection of up to 1 m of sea-level rise per century with cliff calving, and its criticism as an overestimate.
steps.quote: found that the AIS could contribute up to 1 m of sea level rise within a century, if cliff calving is taken into account

steps.action: Restates the question of MICI speed, to be answered with a shear-failure cliff-calving law plus mélange buttressing in place of the step-like parameterization.
steps.quote: We revisit the question of MICI in the AIS using a more complex parameterization of cliff calving

steps.action: Adopts the authors' earlier cliff-calving law (2019) and mélange-buttressing parameterization (2021), which gives an upper bound Cmax on calving set by embayment geometry and mélange properties (Eq. 1).
steps.quote: there is an upper limit to the calving rate

steps.action: Chooses the Amundsen region as the place where MISI and MICI are started, citing paleo plough marks and observed ongoing MISI.
steps.quote: We consider the Amundsen region of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) as the likely initiator of MICI.

steps.action: Bounds the mélange exit velocity from Greenland mélange and Weddell Sea iceberg drift speeds, measures embayment dimensions by hand, and computes Cmax for Thwaites (19.6 km/a), Pine Island (15.5 km/a) and two extreme geometries (Table 1).
steps.quote: by measuring the embayment manually

steps.action: Designs the PISM regional WAIS experiments (REF, BMT at 200 m/a basal melt, FLK floatkill, CC# with fixed Cmax 2-20 km/a, CCA# with Cmax updated every 5 a for exit velocities 10-1000 km/a) and a stand-alone seasonal mélange-freezing experiment with a time-dependent exit velocity (Eq. 2).
steps.quote: Five types of experiments were carried out

steps.action: Runs the MISI experiments; floatkill and basal melt each give about 0.6 m of sea-level rise in 100 a relative to REF.
steps.quote: the two MISI experiments (FLK and BMT) contribute about 0.6 m of sea-level rise within 100 a

steps.action: Compares the MISI result with the 16-model LARMIP-2 ensemble: it lies at the upper end but is not the highest.
steps.quote: This corresponds to the upper limit of the sea-level contribution from the Amundsen sector found in LARMIP-2

steps.action: Checks that the two ways of removing buttressing (floatkill and high basal melt) give similar sea-level contributions, consistent with ABUMIP.
steps.quote: The sea-level contributions resulting from the FLK and BMT experiments are very similar.

steps.action: Runs the MICI experiments; sea-level contribution, calving discharge and calving amplification scale with Cmax, about doubling (CC10) or tripling (CC20) the MISI value and more than fivefold for CCA1000 (Table 2).
steps.quote: MICI can more than double (CC10) or even triple (CC20) the sea-level contribution

steps.action: Attributes the weak effect of small-Cmax cliff calving to PISM's subgrid partially filled margin cells, citing unpublished resolution tests, rather than revising the calving model.
steps.quote: This is because PISM uses a subgrid scheme for the ice margin

steps.action: In the adaptive runs, Cmax falls as the calving front lengthens and the embayments merge, to about one third of its initial value (Table 3, Fig. 6).
steps.quote: the upper bound on calving rate decreases with grounding-line retreat into the Amundsen Basin

steps.action: Fits an exponential relation between normalized Cmax and sea-level contribution across the CCA# runs (Eq. 3).
steps.quote: The relation between calving rate and sea-level contribution can be fitted with

steps.action: Shows that the Cmax decline holds across all five exit velocities from 10 to 1000 km/a (Table 3, Fig. 6).
steps.quote: [...] , C max decreases to about one third of its initial value.

steps.action: Keeps the claim that mélange buttressing grows with retreat, so MICI cannot be arbitrarily fast and slows as it progresses.
steps.quote: MICI cannot be arbitrarily fast and even decelerates as it progresses

steps.action: Analyses grounding-line and ice-divide retreat and retreat rates along the Thwaites and Pine Island flowlines against bed topography (Figs. 7-9).
steps.quote: We examine the retreat along two flowlines

steps.action: Derives the expectation that retreat rate should track bed depth, from superlinear scaling of grounding-line flux (Schoof 2007) and of cliff calving with ice thickness.
steps.quote: We expect bed topography to control grounding-line retreat for two reasons

steps.action: Tests the expectation with Spearman correlation between retreat rate and bed depth: minimal correlation for Pine Island and none for Thwaites (Table 4).
steps.quote: shows only a minimal correlation for Pine Island Glacier and no correlation at all for Thwaites Glacier

steps.action: Explains the failed correlation by auxiliaries (1-D flowline inside 2-D flow, flowline misalignment, flow inertia) instead of rejecting topographic control.
steps.quote: we analyse flow along a 1-dimensional flowline embedded in a more complex 2-dimensional flow

steps.action: Keeps bed topography as a major control of retreat rate, based on qualitative acceleration on retrograde beds and stalls at ridges.
steps.quote: So we can conclude that bed topography is a major control of the rate of grounding-line retreat.

steps.action: Runs the stand-alone mélange model: with zero exit velocity calving is suppressed within about 10 a, but seasonal freezing only modulates calving because the mélange equilibrates over years.
steps.quote: [...] freezing of mélange is not sufficient to stop calving

steps.action: Checks the mélange model's force per unit width at the calving front against the backpressure Crawford et al. (2021) found sufficient to stop calving of a 1000 m cliff.
steps.quote: a similar force per unit width was found when calving is suppressed

steps.action: Keeps the claim that mélange build-up can stop MICI only temporarily, in winter.
steps.quote: would therefore halt MICI only temporarily

steps.action: Lists the limits of the idealized mélange geometry (non-unique conversion, uniform calving, neglected pinning points, prescribed margin, freezing) and proposes a spatially resolved mélange model.
steps.quote: it would be beneficial to use a spatially resolved mélange model

steps.action: Sets the results against the observed re-advance of Sermeq Kujalleq under ocean cooling and stronger mélange buttressing.
steps.quote: increased mélange buttressing at the glacier terminus

steps.action: Compares the simulations with paleo evidence that MICI stopped at a bathymetric ridge during deglaciation; the simulations show only temporary halts at ridges.
steps.quote: our simulations show only temporary halts in grounding-line retreat at bathymetric ridges

steps.action: Concludes that a lengthening calving front with a fixed exit width raises buttressing, lowers Cmax and slows MICI, and that mélange alone is unlikely to stop it.
steps.quote: a decrease in the upper bound on calving rates, and consequently a slowdown in the progress of MICI

tree.answer: MICI, a hypothesized self-reinforcing ice-cliff retreat after ice-shelf loss
No; few observations of cliff-calving glaciers, so it is studied in a model
Bound the speed and sea-level contribution of MISI and MICI and the stabilizing role of mélange buttressing
No stated rival explanations; contrasts are MISI-only versus MISI+MICI and fixed versus adaptive Cmax
Experiments differ in sea-level contribution by Cmax; adaptive runs predict declining Cmax
Conditions set in the model (floatkill, basal melt, Cmax, exit velocity)
Cmax decline persists across exit velocities of 10-1000 km/a; floatkill and basal melt agree; the bed-topography correlation fails
Kept: mélange buttressing slows MICI in the model, explicitly not a quantitative estimate

end.claim: In adaptive PISM simulations of the WAIS, mélange buttressing strengthens as MICI retreats into the Amundsen Basin, lowering the calving-rate bound Cmax to about one third of its initial value (fitted against sea-level contribution, Eq. 3, for exit velocities of 10-1000 km/a) and slowing MICI.

decisive_move.sentence: The adaptive cliff-calving runs, which recompute Cmax from the evolving embayment geometry every 5 model years, are what produce the declining upper bound and hence the slowdown claim.

gates.evidence: The mélange-buttressing hypothesis from the authors' 2021 paper directed the design of the adaptive CCA# experiments, but no data were acquired; the work is a model parameter sweep. The Cmax decline could in principle have failed had the embayment geometry evolved differently, but it follows closely from Eq. 1 and was not tested against independent observations. The bed-topography claim faced a correlation test, failed it, and was kept through auxiliary explanations. Nothing is described as fixed before the runs.

imports.item: Spearman correlation coefficient between retreat rate and bed depth
shear failure of an ice cliff as the basis of the calving law
internal friction of mélange treated as a granular material
linear elastic fracture mechanics model of calving (cited)

limits: No review file or discussion was supplied, so no review sequence is coded, although the paper went through open discussion (Discussion started 12 August 2021). The abstract says the mechanism 'has the potential to stop the instability', while §4.2 ¶4 and §5 ¶4 say mélange can only slow MICI, not stop it; the headline is coded from the Results and Conclusions. The authors disclaim quantitative relevance (§0 ¶1). Inference: the Cmax decline follows largely from the geometry built into Eq. 1 (a longer calving front relative to the exit width), so the test it faced was weak. Sub-claims: the MISI contribution of about 0.6 m in 100 a is an estimate without stated uncertainty (estimate_with_resolution at best); the doubling or tripling with Cmax of 10-20 km/a is a regularity in the explored range; 'bed topography is a major control' is best_explanation, kept after the Spearman test showed no or minimal correlation; 'winter freezing is insufficient to stop MICI' is a model result the authors concede runs contrary to observations, because their mélange equilibrates too slowly. The resolution tests behind the subgrid-cell explanation are 'previously unpublished' and not shown; they are coded as not performed here. Comparisons with LARMIP-2 and ABUMIP are agreement with ensembles, one of which (ABUMIP) includes the first author, and are coded control (performed here) and replication (cited) respectively. Model outputs are available only on request; the code is on Zenodo. composition none_fits: the study is a forced parameter sweep of a model with inherited parameterizations, without rival hypotheses, crucial tests, or new observations, so none of the listed walks applies. The fork over ice-divide migration along flowlines is acknowledged but not taken into account (§3.4 ¶2).

disagreements.target: DeConto and Pollard (2016) step-like cliff-calving parameterization
disagreements.support: Replaces the step function with an exponential shear-failure calving law bounded by mélange buttressing, citing Crawford et al. (2021) for the exponential dependence.
disagreements.quote: parameterized cliff calving with a step-like function that is zero for ice cliffs below the stability limit

disagreements.target: DeConto and Pollard (2016) hydrofracturing as the main mechanism of ice-shelf breakup
disagreements.support: Cites projections that surface melt on the Pine Island Ice Shelf stays far below the 300 mm/a collapse threshold even under RCP8.5 (Trusel et al. 2015), and argues for ocean-driven melt and damage instead.
disagreements.quote: hydrofracturing would probably not be the main mechanism leading to ice-shelf failure in the Amundsen region

disagreements.target: Pollard et al. (2015) assumption that small ice-shelf remnants do not prevent cliff calving
disagreements.support: Argues that the Schoof flux may not apply beyond a flowline setup (Reese et al. 2018b) and that a small shelf may affect the 3-D stress balance at the cliff.
disagreements.quote: This is in contrast to the implementation in

disagreements.target: Wise et al. (2017) paleo evidence that MICI stopped at a bathymetric ridge
disagreements.support: The simulations show only temporary halts at interior bathymetric ridges, not a permanent stop.
disagreements.quote: our simulations show only temporary halts in grounding-line retreat at bathymetric ridges

disagreements.target: Observations of winter mélange freezing stopping calving in Greenland (Medrzycka et al. 2016)
disagreements.support: The stand-alone mélange model does not stop calving under seasonal freezing; the authors attribute the mismatch to the model's slow equilibration rather than disputing the observations.
disagreements.quote: Contrary to observations, in this simplified mélange parameterization, [...] freezing of mélange is not sufficient to stop calving.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Floatkill removal of all floating ice for the cliff-calving experiments
alternatives_considered.reason: Basal melt leaves small ice-shelf remnants that prevent the onset of MICI under the exposed-cliff assumption

alternatives_considered.chosen: Exponential shear-failure cliff-calving law with a mélange-buttressing upper bound
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Step-like parameterization of DeConto and Pollard (2016)
alternatives_considered.reason: More complex, based on shear failure; supported by Crawford et al. (2021)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Cliff calving only at exposed, grounded ice cliffs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Allowing cliff calving behind small ice-shelf remnants (Pollard et al. 2015)
alternatives_considered.reason: Schoof flux may not apply beyond a flowline setup; a small shelf may affect the 3-D stress balance

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both fixed Cmax (CC2-CC20) and adaptive Cmax (CCA10-CCA1000)
Embayment assumed entirely filled with mélange
alternatives_considered.reason: The parameterization cannot evolve the mélange margin, and mélange thickness equilibrates within a few years

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Constraining the cliff-calving scaling parameter C0
alternatives_considered.reason: Cmax dominates the buttressed calving rate, so the uncertainty of C0 is not a major concern

alternatives_considered.chosen: Calving discharge, alongside sea-level contribution, to separate MISI and MICI
alternatives_considered.reason: Floatkill and cliff-calving discharge are reported separately

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Spatially resolved mélange model (e.g. Pollard et al. 2018)
alternatives_considered.reason: A resolved model introduces additional mélange parameters that are difficult to constrain
